title: Unfinished tasks are supposed to stick in memory better than finished ones.
description:
Unfinished tasks are supposed to stick in memory better than finished ones. It is named the Zeigarnik effect, after a 1927 study, and shows up in almost every article about why checklists work.

Psychologist working with Kurt Lewin. She turned an odd detail, a waiter who forgot every order the moment the bill was paid, into a real experiment.

Later attempts to repeat the result kept failing. A 1968 study found no real difference in memory between finished and unfinished tasks.

Researchers found no memory advantage for unfinished tasks at all. Their own conclusion: the Zeigarnik effect lacks universal validity.

A related effect, the urge to go back and finish something, held up fine. That one just never got the famous name.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeigarnik_effect: establishes that Bluma Zeigarnik, a Lithuanian Soviet psychologist working with Kurt Lewin, published the original finding in 1927 in the journal Psychologische Forschung after Lewin noticed a waiter who remembered every unpaid order in detail but forgot them completely once the bill was settled; also records a 1968 replication attempt by Van Bergen that found no significant difference in recall between finished and unfinished tasks, and summarises a 2025 systematic review and meta analysis that found no memory advantage for unfinished tasks.
- https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-025-05000-w: Ghibellini and Meier's 2025 meta analysis itself, whose abstract states they found no memory advantage for unfinished tasks but did find a general tendency to resume interrupted tasks, and concludes that this related effect, named after Zeigarnik's colleague Maria Ovsiankina, represents a genuine general tendency while the Zeigarnik effect itself lacks universal validity.
